Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis. 
            2.2 kubernetes yamls based on the analysis.
            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes 
        4. commit / push to repo

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a practical “recipe” you can follow (or copy‑paste into a script) to get everything done locally and then push the changes back to the remote.  
I’ll walk through each numbered step, show the exact commands you’d run, and point out where the helper functions you listed would fit in.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1.1  Clone the repo into a local folder called nodejs-welcome
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on Windows and don’t have SSH keys set up, you can use HTTPS instead:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the contents & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Analyse the repo

```bash
# 2.1.1  Run the analysis tool (the function you mentioned)
# In practice this would be a CLI command or a script that calls the `analyse_repo_contents` function.
# Example pseudo‑command:
analyse_repo_contents --directory_name . --include_subdirectories true --excluded_files "README.md" "*.md" --language_threshold 10.0
```

> **What you’ll get** – The output will tell you the dominant language(s).  
> For a typical Node.js repo you’ll see something like:

```
{
  "predominant_language": "JavaScript",
  "languages": {
    "JavaScript": 95.3,
    "JSON": 2.1,
    "Markdown": 1.5
  }
}
```

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

```bash
# 2.2.1  Call the helper function (or write your own script)
create_a_docker_file \
  --directory_name . \
  --base_image "node:18-alpine" \
  --maintainer "Your Name <you@example.com>" \
  --port 3000 \
  --commands "npm ci; npm run build"
```

> **Result** – A `Dockerfile` will appear in the repo root.  
> If you prefer to hand‑craft it, here’s a minimal template:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=builder /app/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --production
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
```

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

```bash
# 2.3.1  Call the helper function (or write your own script)
create_kubernetes_yaml_file \
  --directory_name . \
  --deployment_name "nodejs-welcome-deploy" \
  --image_name "your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest" \
  --replicas 3 \
  --service_type "ClusterIP" \
  --port 80 \
  --target_port 3000
```

> **Result** – A `k8s.yaml` (or separate `deployment.yaml` + `service.yaml`) will be written.  
> Sample content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deploy
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Important** – Add two secrets to the repo (`Settings → Secrets → Actions`):  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub login  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a personal access token with `write:packages` scope

---

## 3️⃣ Stage all new/changed files

```bash
# 3.1  Add everything that was created or modified
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

> If you want to be extra cautious, you can run `git status` first to confirm what’s staged.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# 4.1  Commit the changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4.2  Push to the remote
git push origin main
```

> After the push, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the next commit to `main`, building and pushing the Docker image.

---

### Quick recap of the whole process in one shell session

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome

# Analyse (pseudo‑call)
analyse_repo_contents --directory_name . --include_subdirectories true

# Create Dockerfile
create_a_docker_file --directory_name . --base_image "node:18-alpine" --maintainer "Your Name <you@example.com>" --port 3000 --commands "npm ci; npm run build"

# Create Kubernetes YAML
create_kubernetes_yaml_file --directory_name . --deployment_name "nodejs-welcome-deploy" --image_name "your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest" --replicas 3 --service_type "ClusterIP" --port 80 --target_port 3000

# Create GitHub Actions workflow
cat > .github/workflows/build.yml <<'EOF'
name: Build & Push Docker Image
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: \${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: \${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}
      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
EOF

git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! Once the push completes, you’ll see the new files in the GitHub UI, and the Actions tab will show the workflow running. If you hit any snags (e.g., missing secrets, build failures), the logs in the Actions tab will guide you toward the fix. Happy coding!
